claims.text: As-received Q235 steel has a native, non-engineered oxide layer.
Annealing Q235 steel at approximately 700 °C in a low-oxygen atmosphere for 15–30 minutes will induce a tailored oxide film.
The annealing-induced oxide film on Q235 steel will be thin and uniformly distributed.
The annealing-induced film will consist primarily of iron with manganese and silicon enrichment.
The engineered oxide film will act as a barrier against aggressive salt environments.
The oxide film will limit metal-ion dissolution by reducing interaction between the Q235 substrate and the salt environment.
An intact, adherent oxide microstructure will retard corrosion during cyclic room-temperature and approximately 800 °C exposure.
Retention of film cohesion and uniformity at high temperature will inhibit oxidation and mass change.
Film degradation through spallation or porosity development will accelerate corrosion.
Imperfections in the oxide film at room temperature can initiate localized pitting.
Annealed Q235 with a verified uniform film will exhibit less mass change than untreated Q235 under both room-temperature and high-temperature cyclic salt exposure.
Annealed Q235 with a verified uniform film will exhibit lower pitting density than untreated Q235 under both exposure regimes.
Annealed Q235 will show better passivation behavior than the untreated reference.
Oxide-film integrity, thickness, and Fe/Mn/Si ratios govern the protective response of annealed Q235.
Annealing temperature and duration influence the protective surface structure.
Q235's low alloy content makes the precise composition and protective quality of its annealing-induced oxide uncertain.
The proposed mechanism may not extend directly to higher-alloy or stainless steels because their oxide compositions and formation mechanisms differ.

contradictions.description: The mechanism explicitly identifies film degradation as the condition under which protection fails and corrosion accelerates, but the predicted outcome and falsification rule treat observation of film degradation itself as falsifying the hypothesis. Film degradation accompanied by increased corrosion could instead support the proposed failure branch.
